title: Samsung CTO says HBM4 showing ‘good' manufacturing yield - The Korea Times
content: Samsung Electronics Chief Technology Officer Song Jai-hyuk speaks during his keynote speech for SEMICON Korea 2026 at Coex in Seoul, Wednesday. Samsung Electronics Chief Technology Officer Song Jai-hyuk said Wednesday the company’s high-bandwidth memory 4 (HBM4) chip is showing “good” manufacturing yield, adding that clients have expressed strong satisfaction with its performance. Samsung Electronics Chief Technology Officer Song Jai-hyuk speaks to reporters at SEMICON Korea 2026 in southern Seoul, Wednesday. During his keynote speech, Song stressed Samsung Electronics’ advantage as a company capable of foundry, memory and chip packaging businesses, saying it will demonstrate a “distinctive and powerful Samsung-only semiconductor synergy through co-optimization.”. To cope with growing workloads required for AI accelerators, Song said Samsung is considering custom HBM based on a compute-in-base-die architecture, which allows part of the workload typically handled by graphics processing units and other logic chips to be processed by the memory’s base die.

2. Tech & Science
Samsung shows confidence in HBM, portrays next-gen road map
Listen
By Nam Hyun-woo
 Published KST
 Updated KST
CTO says customers ‘very satisfied’ over HBM4 performance
Samsung Electronics Chief Technology Officer Song Jai-hyuk speaks during his keynote speech for SEMICON Korea 2026 at Coex in Seoul, Wednesday. Yonhap
Samsung Electronics Chief Technology Officer Song Jai-hyuk said Wednesday the company’s high-bandwidth memory 4 (HBM4) chip is showing “good” manufacturing yield, adding that clients have expressed strong satisfaction with its performance.
“We may have fallen short of demonstrating our world-class technological responsiveness to customer needs for a while, but this should be seen as a return to that standard,” Song told reporters before his keynote speech for SEMICON Korea 2026 in Seoul.
Samsung reportedly plans to begin HBM4 mass production and shipping to major customers later this month. Its HBM4 chips are using its 1c process, the sixth-generation 10-nanometer-class DRAM technology, for the DRAM cell die, while using a 4-nanometer foundry process for the base die.
Based on these technologies, Samsung had its HBM4 chips achieve data processing speeds of up to 11.7 gigabits per second (Gbps), exceeding the Joint Electron Device Engineering Council’s standard of 8 Gbps.
Since they are the industry’s latest technologies, questions have been raised over how the company will secure production yield as operations ramp up, but Song expressed confidence.
“It is difficult to describe (the yield) in numbers, but I can say the status is very good,” he said, adding that customers are “very satisfied” with the performance of the chip.
“In terms of technology, we believe we remain at the top. The question of how we manage our portfolio falls into the realm of business … We believe our in-house capabilities spanning memory, foundry and packaging create the best environment for making artificial intelligence (AI)-driven products, and the combination is generating synergy.”
Samsung Electronics Chief Technology Officer Song Jai-hyuk speaks to reporters at SEMICON Korea 2026 in southern Seoul, Wednesday. Korea Times photo by Nam Hyun-woo
During his keynote speech, Song stressed Samsung Electronics’ advantage as a company capable of foundry, memory and chip packaging businesses, saying it will demonstrate a “distinctive and powerful Samsung-only semiconductor synergy through co-optimization.”
To cope with growing workloads required for AI accelerators, Song said Samsung is considering custom HBM based on a compute-in-base-die architecture, which allows part of the workload typically handled by graphics processing units and other logic chips to be processed by the memory’s base die. Through this approach, he predicted power efficiency could be improved by up to 2.8 times.
He also introduced a technology dubbed zHBM, in which HBM is stacked vertically on top of logic chips, saying it could deliver another major leap in bandwidth and power efficiency. Under this architecture, bandwidth is expected to increase fourfold, while power consumption could be reduced to one-quarter of current levels.
SK hynix Senior Vice President Lee Sung-hoon also shared the outlook that the semiconductor industry will face unprecedented technological challenges for the next 10 years, and that the industry can find a breakthrough through AI-driven research and data collaboration across the chip ecosystem.
SEMICON Korea, the country’s largest semiconductor industry fair, kicked off its three-day run at Coex in southern Seoul the same day. This year’s edition is the largest of its kind, with more than 550 companies in the semiconductor value chain participating, including Nvidia, Samsung Electronics, SK hynix, Intel, Kioxia, Micron, ASML and Applied Materials. More than 75,000 people have signed up to attend the event, according to SEMI Korea.
Under the theme of Transform Tomorrow, the event will feature more than 30 sessions where over 200 experts and other speakers will discuss advanced manufacturing technologies, AI, market trends and other key topics in the industry.

Campbell-Blackwell is to be based out of the UK, while Wall will operate out of Australia. Both appointments are to come into effect immediately.
With a background in software, Campbell-Blackwell joined Iress as a technical architect almost 16 years ago. Since then, he has risen through the ranks to head of architecture, global head of platform engineering, group head of architecture and core services, and UK CTO. 
In a statement announcing the appointment, Iress notes that Campbell-Blackwell will help "drive the next phase of growth", which will involve platform modernisation as it embeds AI across its product suite. "Elevating the CTO role reflects the importance of technology execution in delivering this next phase," adds Iress group CEO and managing director Andrew Russell.

At the same time, Iress has also appointed Sam Wall as CEO of its APAC Wealth business on a permanent basis. Wall had been serving in an acting capacity since February 2026, taking over from Kelli Willmer, who had held the role for the past two and a half years.
Founded in 1993, Iress is a software provider that offers fintechs, challenger banks, traders, investment managers, and more a range of trading and market data, sourcing software and financial advice software, including its flagship Xplan solution.

Colorado is looking to hire its next chief technology officer (CTO), to fill the position after its former CTO departed for a role with Oregon government.  
Alex Pettit stepped down in November to serve as Oregon’s digital transformation projects director, the state where he had been CIO from January 2014 to June 2018. He had been CTO in Colorado since January 2020 and had also previously served as CIO for the state of Oklahoma.  
“We’re just looking for a leader who can help us continue to evolve and improve much of the ways Alex set us up,” CIO David Edinger said.  
The state posted the CTO job listing Tuesday, and it closes on Dec. 22. More than 70 percent of the state’s Office of Information Technology (OIT) staff report to the CTO, Edinger said.  
In OIT, the CTO is charged with defining and shaping the office’s service delivery, supporting agencies with deep technical expertise, and aligning IT standards across all state government entities on matters like applications and data, according to the job listing.  
The move to Oregon government marked a “return home” for Pettit, as he shared in a LinkedIn post.  
“I’m honored to once again contribute to Oregon’s technology future — helping modernize legacy platforms, evolve our enterprise architecture, and prepare for the demands ahead,” Pettit wrote.  
Although the technology talent market can be challenging, with private-sector organizations sometimes attracting talent more easily — largely due to greater flexibility and pay — than those in the public sector, Edinger said the opposite is true right now. As such, he expects to see ”some really great talent” apply for the CTO role.

title: The first 100 days as a scale-up fintech CTO: A roadmap - FinTech Futures
content: # The first 100 days as a scale-up fintech CTO: A roadmap. A practical roadmap for navigating the first 100 days as a scale-up fintech CTO with clarity and confidence. The scale-up fintech CTO role is not a variant of the start-up or enterprise CTO role. The start-up CTO’s primary obligation is survival through velocity. The scale-up CTO must do both simultaneously, with a team hired for one and asked to do the other, within a regulatory environment that has become markedly less forgiving as the company’s balance sheet grows. A wrong entry in a ledger is a regulatory event. The new CTO is not joining a team. Before the first day, read the most recent board pack, the most recent regulatory correspondence, and the last six months of post-mortems. The primary output of the first ten days is a clear, private map of what has been inherited. Treating regulatory engineering as the compliance team’s problem is the most common and most expensive mistake a new fintech CTO makes.

The first 100 days as a scale-up fintech CTO: A roadmap
A practical roadmap for navigating the first 100 days as a scale-up fintech CTO with clarity and confidence.
Ben Y.,
BSc, MBA | Fintech CTO
September 2, 2026
schedule
6 Min Read
The scale-up fintech CTO role is not a variant of the start-up or enterprise CTO role. It is its own creature, with distinct failure modes.
The start-up CTO’s primary obligation is survival through velocity. The enterprise CTO’s is stability through governance. The scale-up CTO must do both simultaneously, with a team hired for one and asked to do the other, within a regulatory environment that has become markedly less forgiving as the company’s balance sheet grows.
Three things distinguish this context. First, the technical debt inherited was not incurred recklessly; it was incurred deliberately by a team trying to survive. Treating it with contempt loses the room immediately.
Second, financial systems have a different relationship with correctness than most software. A wrong pixel in a UI is annoying. A wrong entry in a ledger is a regulatory event. The engineering culture must reflect this asymmetry.
Related:
FinTech Futures: Top five news stories of the week – 28 August 2026
Third, the company almost certainly grew its engineering team faster than its engineering practices. The new CTO is not joining a team. They are joining a collection of sub-teams that may barely know each other.
Before the first day, read the most recent board pack, the most recent regulatory correspondence, and the last six months of post-mortems. These three documents reveal more about the real state of the organisation than any onboarding deck.
Days 1 to 10: Observe without touching
The most expensive mistake a new CTO can make is acting before they understand. The primary output of the first ten days is a clear, private map of what has been inherited. Nothing ships, nothing changes, no processes are announced.
Schedule one-to-ones broadly: every engineering team lead, but also the head of compliance, the head of risk, the CFO, and at least two front-line customer support representatives. Attend the first sprint demos as a silent observer. Watch team dynamics rather than evaluating outputs. Ask every engineer the same diagnostic question: if you could change one thing about how we build software here, what would it be? Shadow an on-call engineer for at least one shift. What fails at three in the morning tells more than any architecture diagram.
Read every post-mortem from the past 12 months and note the ratio of time to detect versus time to diagnose versus time to resolve. Review the most recent penetration test report: unresolved high-severity findings older than six months are a governance failure, not a backlog item. Read the regulatory licence documentation directly rather than relying on a summary from the compliance team.
Related:
FinTech Futures: Top five news stories of the week – 21 August 2026
Most importantly, read all contracts with sponsor banks, BaaS providers, card networks, and payment scheme participants. These agreements contain technical covenants with legal and financial teeth. Breaches have triggered partnership terminations on 30 days’ notice. Know what has been signed before touching any integration.
Days 11 to 30: Structured diagnosis
Before claiming to improve engineering capability, establish a baseline. Establish a baseline using the current DORA five pillars, supplemented by fintech-specific measures for risk, reporting, resilience, third-party, and sharing. Baselines announced before measurement are aspirations that will be gamed.
Assess six domains directly: production reliability, data integrity, security posture, deployment and testing discipline, observability, and engineering unit economics. The data integrity domain deserves particular attention in fintech. In most software, a bug causes a bad user experience. In a payment or lending system, a bug can cause incorrect account balances, duplicate charges, or misreported regulatory figures. Some of these are recoverable. Some require regulatory notification. The threshold for mandatory reporting is almost always lower than the engineering team assumes.
Related:
FinovateFall 2026 is leading the way with fintech innovation
Map every compliance obligation to the specific system and team currently responsible for fulfilling it. Most scale-up fintechs will find this mapping does not exist in one place. Building it is itself a diagnostic act. Treating regulatory engineering as the compliance team’s problem is the most common and most expensive mistake a new fintech CTO makes. It is an engineering problem and must be owned as such.
Days 31 to 60: First interventions
By day 30, there is enough information to act. The interventions chosen in this phase define credibility with the engineering team more than any town hall or strategy document. They must be genuinely valuable, attributable to a real diagnosis, and completable within 30 days.
If any engineers represent single points of failure for production knowledge, address this immediately. Pair those engineers with at least one other person on the work and formalise the knowledge transfer. If the on-call rotation is falling disproportionately on a small number of engineers, fix it. Formalise the rotation, improve alerting quality to reduce noise, and give the team explicit permission to spend time reducing alert volume. Pick one reliability problem engineers have flagged and product has deprioritised and fix it.
By day 45, present to the board. This is not a strategy presentation. It is an honesty presentation. Share the DORA baselines without apology. Present the top three technical risks with explicit owners and timelines. Propose a technical investment budget that distinguishes between capability investment, reliability investment, and compliance investment. Most boards have never seen this distinction made explicitly. Boards forgive problems they were warned about. They do not forgive surprises that could have been disclosed.
Days 61 to 100: Foundation and forward roadmap
By day 90, a technology strategy document should be taking shape. This is not a product roadmap or a list of initiatives. It is a narrative answering three questions: where is the engineering organisation now? What does it need to become to support the company’s next growth phase? And what are the explicit trade-offs being made to get there? The trade-offs section is the most valuable and most frequently omitted part. Naming trade-offs explicitly - choosing platform reliability over feature velocity in the first two quarters, for example - eliminates the passive conflict between engineering and product that occurs when these choices are left implicit.
Address the build-versus-buy decision framework explicitly. In fintech, the temptation to build everything is high, and the cost of maintaining what has been built is almost always underestimated. The strategy should define what is core to the business’s differentiation, what is necessary but not differentiating, and what is best achieved through partnership.
At day 100, the architecture will not be solved. The technical debt will not be eliminated. The team needed will not yet be hired. None of that is realistic, and claiming it as a benchmark sets up failure. What should exist by day 100 is a complete, honest picture of technical health shared with the board and leadership team without omission, measured baselines rather than aspirational ones, risk reduction started on the highest-priority exposures, every compliance obligation mapped to a specific system and owner, and an 18-month technology strategy with explicit trade-offs approved by the board.
The job at day 100 is not to have fixed the system. It is to have earned the trust to fix it - from the engineering team, from the board, and from the regulators who are watching how the institution manages its technology risk.

Brian Wagner joins ValidPath operator Rimbal as CTO
Wagner will work alongside Brad Powar, who had served as the company's CTO since August 2019 before rising to chief AI technologist earlier this month.
Tyler Pathe,
Reporter, FinTech Futures
March 25, 2026
1 Min Read
Image: Rimbal
Brian Wagner has joined Rimbal, the parent group of independent financial adviser (IFA) network ValidPath, as the company's new chief technology officer (CTO). 
In his new role, Rimbal, headquartered in the UK, says Wagner will "focus on scalability, enterprise robustness, AI-grade data sovereignty, and building the technological foundations for enabling in-house and third-party adviser, client, and agentic systems and applications".
ValidPath provides a central network that manages compliance, back-office technology, and professional indemnity insurance for IFAs, alongside specialised funding and transition support to help advisers grow or manage business succession.
The business was founded in 2002 and was acquired by Rimbal from founder and majority shareholder Kevin Andrew Moss in June 2018. 
Wagner is already familiar with the CTO role, having previously served in the position for cybersecurity firms Bulletproof and Defense.com, and most recently, for tax recovery company Revenir since the start of 2023.

Prior to this, Wagner spent over six years at Amazon Web Services (AWS), where he worked across a variety of compliance-focused positions, including head of compliance EMEA for AWS Financial Services.
He will work at Rimbal alongside Brad Powar, who had served as the company's CTO since August 2019 before rising to chief AI technologist earlier this month.
